entities.summary:
Jehu, the tenth monarch of the Northern Kingdom of Israel, ascended to power in approximately 841 BCE through a violent coup, reigning for 28 years until around 814 BCE. His reign marks a pivotal, albeit brutal, turning point in Israelite history, primarily remembered for the complete extermination of the Omride dynasty and a sweeping purge of Baal worship from the kingdom. Anointed by a prophet sent by Elisha, Jehu acted as a divinely sanctioned instrument of judgment against the house of Ahab, whose syncretistic religious policies had deeply offended the Yahwist faction in Israel.

The core of Jehu's actions began with the assassination of King Joram of Israel and King Ahaziah of Judah at Jezreel. This was swiftly followed by the brutal killing of Queen Mother Jezebel and the systematic slaughter of Ahab's seventy sons in Samaria, effectively eradicating the Omride lineage. His religious zeal culminated in a cunning ruse where he gathered all Baal worshippers under the pretense of a grand sacrifice, only to have them massacred within the temple of Baal in Samaria, subsequently destroying the temple itself. Despite this internal consolidation of Yahwist authority, Jehu also faced external pressures, notably submitting to the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III, as depicted on the Black Obelisk, a testament to his kingdom's diminished geopolitical standing.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jehu's violent accession and subsequent purges fundamentally reshaped the religious and political landscape of the Northern Kingdom of Israel, ending the Omride dynasty and securing the preeminence of Yahwism, though at the cost of weakening the kingdom against Aramean aggression.
